The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us
Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?

Nikhil Sharma† Email: nsharm27@jhu.edu    Kelly Marchisio‡ Email: kelly@cohere.com    Kenton Murray Email: kenton@jhu.edu    Ziang Xiao† Email: ziang.xiao@jhu.edu    †Johns Hopkins University       ‡ Cohere       George Mason University
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce NarrativeBench, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users’ control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. NarrativeBench provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/jhu-clsp/narrative-bench
Code: https://github.com/isle-dev/Narrative-Bench-NeurIPS-2026

1 Introduction

We, informavores [36], seek and consume information continually to find what we need to know, decide, or act on. Despite information today being more accessible, navigation has grown harder. New information is produced at a scale and speed no information seeker can track, and what exists is fragmented across geographic and linguistic silos, each with its own vocabulary, claims, framings, and emphases. Throughout history, we have built information systems, from libraries to search engines and social media feeds, to help us navigate the complex information world. However, these systems often reproduce, and sometimes amplify, the very problems they were meant to solve. By organizing content around a user’s query language, region, and prior behavior, they create filter bubbles [45, 46, 26] and echo chambers [11, 1], increasing polarization and weakening the common ground necessary for democratic stability [16]. For an information seeker, overcoming these barriers is costly: it requires knowing which foreign perspectives to search for, translating conflicting sources, and identifying missing vocabulary and information silos.

Large Language Models (LLMs) hold promise as a new kind of information system. In principle, their multilingual, conversational, and reasoning capabilities should let a user ask a question in any language from any region and receive an answer that synthesizes across the perspectives available, bridging cultural divides and improving democratic deliberation [57]. But are LLMs actually helping us navigate this complex information world? A growing body of research auditing linguistic, political, and cultural biases in LLMs suggests they may instead reproduce and exacerbate the barriers they are meant to overcome. Those models create generative echo chambers by reinforcing user beliefs [52, 15, 40, 51, 10, 22], prefer information in the query language over more relevant foreign sources [53, 27], and struggle to reason when evidence contains explicit conflicts [56, 54, 67, 53]. Whether LLMs can serve as information systems that break, rather than reinforce, the traditional barriers of information seeking remains an open question.

In this paper, we identify three foundational information seeking capabilities that give users control over which narratives an LLM presents: requesting a particular narrative, excluding a narrative, and identifying perspectives missing from an answer. Building on the foundational capabilities, we evaluate three higher-level information seeking capabilities: presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. We evaluate the capabilities across contested topics, including geopolitical conflicts where the stakes of navigation failure are high. Recent global conflicts underscore the urgency: Israel–Palestine, India–Pakistan, and Russia–Ukraine are not only fought through military and diplomatic action, but also through parallel information environments in which different regional and linguistic communities encounter different accounts of the same events [26, 55, 17]. Information flows in such geopolitical conflicts consist of culturally situated accounts with differing causal and moral interpretations of the same event [14, 35], making information seeking challenging. Information seekers in such environments need to navigate and parse diverging information streams across languages, making translation alone insufficient. We formulate this challenge as the problem of navigating diverse multilingual narratives. In this paper, narratives are defined as culturally situated accounts of events that interpret the actions and intentions of those involved [6], and operationalized as accounts of a topic expressed in a particular language by sources anchored in a geographic region. However, we acknowledge that narratives vary even within the same geographic region and language. Our operationalization simplifies this complexity to provide an auditable unit for measuring how information systems allow users to navigate diverse information streams. We argue that an information system’s ability to navigate narratives as operationalized in this paper is a necessary but not sufficient condition for enabling diverse multilingual information seeking. Future work should extend this operationalization to capture narrative differences within regions and languages.

To evaluate the foundational and higher-level information seeking capabilities, we introduce NarrativeBench, an ecologically grounded dataset and benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. The evaluation covers 4,800 cases across 24 query languages (Appendix B.1).

We find that current multilingual LLMs (1) struggle to distinguish and selectively present different perspectives, (2) fail to consistently present diverse views across languages, (3) vary in narrative coverage between neutral and confirmatory queries, and (4) perform unevenly across languages. Such capability gaps decrease exposure to diverse narratives and hinder effective information seeking, potentially exacerbating linguistic filter bubbles and echo chambers, reducing common ground across regions, and amplifying existing conflicts and divisions in societies.

Overall, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We formulate diverse multilingual information seeking as a problem of navigating narratives and identify foundational and higher-level capabilities LLMs need to help users navigate diverse perspectives across languages and regions.

  • •

    We introduce NarrativeBench, an ecologically grounded dataset and benchmark to evaluate the information seeking capabilities of multilingual LLMs.

  • •

    We provide an empirical analysis of state-of-the-art LLMs, identifying capability gaps that hinder diverse information seeking across languages and regions.

NarrativeBench provides a capability-grounded foundation for building information systems that promote equitable information access, reduce polarization, and enhance democratic discourse.

2 Related Work

2.1 Diverse Information Seeking and Perspective Exposure

Information seeking depends on the information available and the perspectives users encounter, select, and trust. Research on selective exposure and partisan news consumption shows that some audiences concentrate their attention on politically aligned sources [2, 38]; strong political beliefs and the perceived strength of an issue can further increase susceptibility to confirmation bias during news consumption [5]. Efforts to broaden perspective exposure include interfaces that help users explore news and opinions across political positions [24], but explicitly labeling the stance of news articles can intensify users’ selection of viewpoints aligned with their beliefs [18]. System choices about information exposure can also influence political attitudes: reducing the prominence of posts expressing antidemocratic attitudes and partisan animosity in news feeds can reduce affective polarization [48]. Experiments with LLM-mediated search show that users exhibit greater confirmation bias in their queries than with conventional search [52]. Biased model responses can further influence users’ judgments by reinforcing existing beliefs or shifting attitudes toward the model’s position [10, 23]. Supporting diverse information seeking therefore requires LLMs to surface relevant missing perspectives even when users ask confirmatory questions and do not explicitly request alternative views.

2.2 LLM-Mediated Information Access and Pluralism

LLMs are increasingly used for information seeking and decision making [8]. LLM-mediated systems shape access to perspectives by selecting sources, synthesizing claims, and deciding which information to include in their responses. Research on AI search and news consumption shows that citations can concentrate on a small set of outlets [68] and identifies concerns about accuracy, transparency, and shared understanding [43, 30]. Existing information-seeking benchmarks evaluate the accuracy and usefulness of retrieved evidence, the completeness of information collection, and reasoning and clarification in expert consultations [64, 62, 28, 69, 13]. Complementary work examines how models identify and distinguish perspectives, represent narrative frames, and accommodate diverse human preferences [9, 42, 29, 44].

Evaluating perspective diversity in information seeking requires examining how query language and the available evidence shape the perspectives presented in model responses. Li et al. [31] show that LLMs answer territorial-dispute questions differently depending on query language, and knowledge-conflict work studies how models behave when context conflicts with parametric memory or when retrieved passages contradict one another [67, 21, 63, 65]. The focus on language-dependent positions and conflicting facts leaves open how models represent competing narratives that emphasize different facts and interpretations of the same event across languages and regions.

2.3 Multilingual LLMs and Information Capabilities

Navigating diverse narratives requires information capabilities that enable access to perspectives across languages. Multilingual LLMs offer a foundation for cross-cultural information seeking, yet current evaluations find inconsistent answers to semantically equivalent questions and performance differences across languages, scripts, and resource levels [60, 3, 66, 20, 7]. Culturally grounded benchmarks evaluate everyday knowledge [39] and knowledge and reasoning through local examination questions [50]. Multilingual question-answering evaluations use information-seeking questions collected directly in diverse languages to assess passage selection and answer extraction [12].

Access to diverse narratives across languages also depends on which sources models select and use in their responses. In multilingual retrieval-augmented generation, where models answer questions using retrieved sources, Sharma et al. [53] find preferences for documents in the query language during retrieval and generation, and for higher-resource languages during generation when query-language evidence is unavailable. Related work identifies preferences for high-resource languages, English, and Latin scripts [47, 61]; models can also favor a source’s language over its relevance [27]. Multilingual benchmarks evaluate answer generation using Wikipedia sources [58], while healthcare audits examine language disparities in factual correctness and response quality [19, 25]. Language preferences can therefore shape which narratives remain available to users even when the evidence is multilingual, motivating evaluation of the diversity represented in the resulting answers. NarrativeBench builds on research in multilingual information access and conflicting evidence by evaluating whether models can selectively present and recover narratives, broaden exposure under confirmatory queries, and maintain comparable information access across languages.

3 NarrativeBench: The Dataset

Gathering the Narratives

We construct NarrativeBench by collecting news articles through localized searches about contested topics. Dataset curation followed four stages: (1) selecting contested topics across regions and languages, (2) identifying regions and stakeholders relevant to each topic, (3) developing region-specific search terms in the relevant languages, and (4) collecting relevant articles and their URLs from the search results. The corpus contains 1,333 news articles from 43 countries, regions, and regional organizations across 23 topics and 23 publication languages. Within each topic, we group articles by source perspective and publication language, yielding 180 narrative groups. Article texts have a median length of 4,654 characters (mean = 5,977, SD = 5,283, range = 610–46,252). We describe the article collection in Appendix A.

Dataset Diagnostics

To assess whether the collection captures distinct narratives, we compared multilingual embeddings of all 1,333 article texts in their publication languages, restricting comparisons to articles about the same topic. Articles within the same narrative group were more similar than articles from different groups (mean cosine similarity difference = 0.047, 95% bootstrap CI [0.044, 0.051], permutation p<0.001p<0.001). After restricting comparisons to articles published in the same language, articles from the same source perspective remained more similar on average than articles from different perspectives (Appendix A.2).

Sourcing Queries for Evaluation

To ground evaluation in naturally occurring information seeking, we assembled 460 queries, comprising 283 questions gathered from Reddit and 177 context-specific adaptations. Reddit queries were gathered through topic-specific searches; adaptations addressed 12 topics with limited query coverage and were reviewed for fidelity to the source question, topic, and intended framing. Two independent annotators rated a sample of 100 English queries on how likely a person would be to ask the question to an AI assistant, giving mean ratings of 4.09 and 4.89 out of 5; neither annotator rated a query as unlikely or very unlikely.

To test whether models preserve access to diverse narratives when queries favor an existing belief, we include 230 neutral and 230 confirmatory queries. Neutral queries request information without endorsing a particular answer, while confirmatory queries seek support for an expressed or implied belief, interpretation, solution, or outcome. Comparing narrative coverage across query categories tests the robustness needed to limit reinforcement of echo chambers during information seeking [52, 41].

Query Translation

To compare information capabilities across query languages, we provide query versions in all 23 publication languages and in Thai. We prepared the translations using Google Translate. The dataset provides 11,038 query–language versions across 24 languages; Appendix A.4 lists the query and publication languages.

We assessed translation quality on a subset covering eight target languages. For 1,704 English-to-target translations, mean WMT22-COMETKiwi-DA scores [49] ranged from 0.853 to 0.879 across the eight languages. Independent annotators also reviewed 40 query–translation pairs selected across languages and COMETKiwi score bands, providing 132 ratings. Annotators found that translations preserved meaning in 90.8% of the ratings they could assess (118/130) and that the queries were likely to be asked by a person in 89.0% (113/127).

4 NarrativeBench: An Information Seeking Benchmark

4.1 Evaluating Information Seeking Capabilities

NarrativeBench is a capability-grounded benchmark for developing models that help people navigate diverse information flows. Following the Evidence-Centered Benchmark Design framework of Liu et al. [33], we connect challenges in information seeking to three foundational and three higher-level capabilities, then define tasks and measures that make the required behavior evaluable.

Foundational Information Seeking Capabilities ( ): Can models include, exclude, and identify missing narratives?

To enable diverse information seeking, models must provide users with affordances for navigating diverse multilingual narratives. A user should be able to request a specific narrative, exclude a specific narrative, or ask which perspectives are missing from a prior answer. We evaluate the foundational capabilities through three tasks:

FC-1: Narrative Inclusion (NI) requires models to present a designated narrative when users request a particular perspective. The task asks the model to include the target narrative and exclude other narratives; expected responses cite evidence only from the target narrative.

FC-2: Narrative Exclusion (NE) requires models to exclude a specified narrative when users seek alternative perspectives. The task asks the model to answer while excluding the target narrative; expected responses cite evidence from the remaining relevant narratives and avoid citing evidence from the target narrative.

FC-3: Missing Narrative Identification (MNI) requires models to identify perspectives omitted from a prior answer. The task presents an answer focused on a narrative and asks the model to revise it by incorporating omitted narratives; expected responses cite evidence from those narratives.

Higher-Level Information Seeking Capabilities

Building on the foundational capabilities, models must broaden access to narratives across filter bubbles, echo chambers, and linguistic disparities.

HC-1 ( ): Can models present diverse narratives from multilingual evidence? To broaden exposure beyond linguistic filter bubbles [53], models must present narratives from diverse multilingual sources. To test narrative diversity in model responses, we compare two conditions: a Baseline Prompt (BP) asks the model to answer the query using the provided evidence; a Diverse Prompt (DP) additionally requests the diverse narratives present in the document context. Narrative coverage under both conditions and the change following an explicit diversity request show how consistently models broaden the perspectives available to users.

HC-2 ( ): Do models preserve narrative coverage under confirmatory queries? To limit reinforcement of confirmation bias and echo chambers [52], models must maintain access to relevant narratives when queries favor a particular viewpoint. We test robustness to confirmatory framing by comparing narrative coverage under neutral and confirmatory queries in the BP and DP conditions.

HC-3 ( ): Do models provide comparable access to narratives across languages? Information seekers should have comparable access to relevant narratives regardless of their query language or the languages of the available sources. We operationalize information parity along two axes: performance across the languages in which users ask, and performance across the languages in which narratives are expressed. Comparable access requires both strong narrative coverage and small performance differences across query and narrative languages.

4.2 Evaluation Metrics and Protocol

Setup

Each evaluation case contains a document context, a user query, and a task instruction. The document context contains three articles from each selected narrative, defined by source perspective and publication language; the same articles are used for each question across tasks and query languages. Models answer in the query language and cite document IDs supporting their claims. For MNI, every model receives the same prior answer focused on one narrative and revises it to include missing perspectives. Appendix B.1 details case construction, localized instructions, and prior answers.

Evaluating the Presence of a Narrative

We identify represented narratives through citations to the provided articles: a narrative is present when the response cites at least one article associated with that narrative. Citations also allow users to inspect the evidence and explore unfamiliar information streams. Article IDs, such as [D001], reveal no source-region or language information. We assess the use of citations as a metric through a human audit of citation support (Appendix C.1).

Narrative Precision, Recall, and F1

We compare the cited narratives, CiC_{i}, with the required narratives, GiG_{i}, for each case. The required set contains the target narrative for NI, all context narratives except the target for NE, the narratives omitted from the prior answer for MNI, and all context narratives for BP and DP. Precision measures whether cited narratives belong to the required set; recall measures coverage of required narratives; F1 summarizes both. NI and NE use F1 to measure users’ control over narrative selection, requiring coverage of requested narratives while penalizing citations to narratives the user asked to omit. MNI uses recall to assess recovery of omitted narratives; BP and DP use recall to assess how broadly an answer covers the available perspectives.

HC-1: Narrative Coverage and Robustness

We measure recall under BP and DP and their paired difference, ΔDP−BP=RDP−RBP\Delta_{\mathrm{DP-BP}}=R_{\mathrm{DP}}-R_{\mathrm{BP}}, holding the question, query language, and document context fixed. The comparison captures the breadth of narratives users receive by default and the additional coverage gained by explicitly asking for diversity.

HC-2: Robustness to Confirmatory Queries

We pool recall across BP and DP, measure the absolute difference between neutral and confirmatory queries for each configuration, then average the gaps across configurations. The gap measures how consistently users can access diverse narratives when seeking confirmation of a preferred viewpoint. We also compare the gaps across query languages and across the five tasks using each task’s primary score. Appendix B.4 examines whether coverage is higher or lower under confirmatory queries after accounting for topic, query language and prompt.

HC-3: Language Disparity

We measure disparity along two axes to distinguish differences associated with the language users ask in from differences associated with the languages of the narratives they seek. For each configuration, we compare mean primary scores in each language with English, Δℓ=Mℓ−Men\Delta_{\ell}=M_{\ell}-M_{\mathrm{en}}. Query-language comparisons pool all five tasks. Target narrative-language comparisons pool NI and NE by the target narrative’s publication language. We average the absolute gaps equally across non-English languages for each configuration and then average the disparities across the 15 configurations.

Source-language omission

Omission rates identify source languages that disappear from responses even when evidence in those languages is available. In BP and DP, each publication language present in the context counts as one opportunity per response. An omission occurs when the response cites no valid in-context document in that language. We divide omissions by opportunities separately for each prompt. To compare matching and other query languages, we pair versions of the same question with identical article contexts and average its other-language versions before comparing omission rates (Appendix B.5). This diagnostic uses citations independently of response-language validation.

Language Validation (LVal)

To measure narrative access in the language requested by the user, we compare each response’s language with the query language and assign a score of zero when they differ; responses in the requested language proceed to narrative scoring (Appendix B.3).

5 Results: How well can LLMs enable diverse
information seeking across multilingual narratives?

We evaluate 14 models under 15 configurations on the same 4,800 cases, yielding 72,000 scored responses. Every configuration includes 960 cases per task, 200 cases per query language, and 2,400 cases per query category. The panel covers all 460 queries, comprising 230 neutral and 230 confirmatory queries. The model set includes Qwen3.5, GPT-OSS, Gemma 4, DeepSeek V4, Gemini, GPT, Kimi, and Command A. Our model selection supports comparisons of model size, base versus instruction-tuned models, and reasoning settings. Appendix B.2 reports model identities, reasoning settings and output budgets.

5.1 Foundational Capabilities: Models lack capabilities necessary for information seeking

Current models show substantial gaps across all three foundational capabilities needed to enable diverse information seeking. Across the 15 configurations, narrative inclusion (NI) achieves a mean F1 of 19.9% (SE = 0.6%), compared with 49.3% (SE = 0.6%) for narrative exclusion (NE); missing narrative identification (MNI) achieves a mean recall of 56.8% (SE = 0.6%). NI F1 is lower than NE F1 in every configuration. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest NI F1 at 52.5% (SE = 1.3%) and MNI recall at 82.8% (SE = 0.7%); Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves the highest NE F1 at 74.2% (SE = 0.7%).

5.2 Higher Level Information Seeking Capabilities

HC-1 Filter Bubbles ( ): Models offer limited coverage across diverse narratives

Models leave substantial gaps in their coverage of the narratives available in multilingual contexts. Narrative recall averages 44.3% (SE = 0.7%) under baseline prompting (BP) and 49.2% (SE = 0.7%) under diverse prompting (DP). Figure 1D compares recall with English for each query language under both prompts. Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves the highest recall under both conditions, reaching 70.6% (SE = 0.9%) under BP and 74.9% (SE = 0.8%) under DP. Even after an explicit diversity request, the strongest configuration leaves one quarter of available narratives unrepresented, limiting how far models broaden exposure beyond linguistic filter bubbles.

HC-2 Echo Chambers ( ): Narrative coverage varies across query framings

Across the 15 configurations, the mean absolute difference in BP/DP narrative recall between neutral and confirmatory queries is 3.23 percentage points. Differences range from 0.32 points for Qwen3.5 9B IT to 10.09 points for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Task-specific gaps are largest for NI F1 at 3.41 points, followed by BP recall at 3.32, DP recall at 3.30, NE F1 at 2.72, and MNI recall at 2.43. Figure 1C shows differences from English in the size of the framing gap for each query language. Table 2 shows that a response can cite more narratives while affirming the query’s premise.

HC-3 Linguistic Disparity ( ): Models offer uneven access to narratives across languages

Across the 15 configurations, mean absolute performance gaps from English are 8.74 percentage points for query languages and 7.51 for target narrative languages. Figure 1A and B show signed gaps from English for each language. Query-language gaps range from 3.59 points for Kimi K2.6 to 13.84 for GPT-OSS 20B (low reasoning). Target narrative-language gaps range from 2.76 points for Qwen3.5 0.8B IT to 10.72 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Under DP, omission rates for Tigrinya, Nepali, and Armenian sources exceed English by 59.8, 57.9 and 54.6 percentage points, respectively (Figure 1E). Consistent with Sharma et al. [53], across BP and DP, models omitted available sources less often when the query language matched the source language (Appendix Figure 2).

6 Discussion

Information capability gaps and the illusion of control.

Conversational systems offer accessible ways to seek information, yet our results show that users cannot reliably direct which narratives models present or recover perspectives that an answer omits. Information seekers revise their questions as they encounter new evidence [4]; users who know which perspective to pursue need the model to isolate it from the surrounding evidence, while users who do not know which perspectives exist need the model to identify omissions. Explicit diversity requests improve coverage, but even the strongest configuration provides cited coverage in the requested language for only about three quarters of available narratives. A response that appears to follow the user’s instruction can consequently offer less control over the information presented than the interface suggests, creating an illusion of control for users who cannot see the missing perspectives [59, 37].

Model development must target information capabilities.

Model development should treat the information seeking capabilities defined in this paper as explicit training and evaluation objectives. The uneven gains from model size, instruction tuning, and reasoning settings suggest that improvements in narrative coverage do not consistently translate into greater control over which narratives users receive. Training should therefore reward responses that follow requests to include, exclude, and recover narratives while covering the relevant evidence. Evaluation should examine whether gains in each capability hold across neutral and confirmatory queries and across languages, connecting model improvements to the information access and control users need.

Response policies also shape information access.

Information access depends on whether a system will answer a query as well as which narratives it presents: the Kimi K2.6 service rejected 552 of 4,800 requests as high risk, with rejections concentrated in topics including India–China tensions, Taiwan, and student protests in India. People relying on different services may therefore face different restrictions on investigating the same topic, making comparable information access across providers necessary for building common ground.

Information parity is necessary for common ground.

Even with multilingual sources supplied and an explicit request for diversity, omission rates for Tigrinya, Nepali, and Armenian sources were about 55–60 percentage points higher than for English when those languages were available (Figure 1E); such gaps can leave people discussing the same issue with access to different accounts. AI mediation can help people find common ground by incorporating participants’ critiques into shared statements [57]; meaningful deliberation also requires access to the competing accounts from which people form their judgments. Information systems that repeatedly omit regional and linguistic perspectives risk narrowing that shared evidence and weakening the common ground needed for democratic discourse [16]. Policy and procurement standards should require reporting of narrative-access disparities across languages and topics, while open models and shared evaluation resources can give communities a practical basis for inspecting and improving information access.

Beyond contested public topics.

Scientific research also depends on navigating diverse narratives, as disciplines may study the same phenomenon using different terms, methods, and standards of evidence. As LLM use in scientific writing grows [32] and extends to literature discovery and synthesis [34], researchers need to request evidence from a particular discipline, set aside an approach they have already reviewed, or discover a line of work a synthesis overlooked. A research assistant that draws mainly on the literature most accessible to the model can make a field appear more settled or uniform than the available evidence warrants.

Policy development and large organizations similarly depend on navigating narratives distributed across disciplines, teams, and regions. Technical teams, regulators, and affected communities may explain the same policy issue differently, while regional teams may hold evidence absent from headquarters’ records. Information systems need to help decision-makers inspect each account, identify missing perspectives, and trace competing claims to their sources. Adapting NarrativeBench to those settings would allow researchers to evaluate whether a synthesis preserves the perspectives and evidence needed for an informed decision.

7 Limitations and Future Directions

Narrative representation.

We group articles by source perspective and publication language to evaluate access to diverse narratives, while accounts within a region or language can differ in the events, causes, and consequences they emphasize. Extending narrative representation to capture disagreement within each narrative group would support a fuller evaluation of how models navigate competing accounts.

Corpus representativeness and multimodal sources.

Our corpus reflects the contested topics, regional sources, and article texts accessible through localized searches. However, information seeking is more complex, it happens across modalities and information mediums. Broader sampling across media formats, regions, and less accessible information streams would help establish how the observed capability gaps vary with the narratives and evidence available to a system.

Source quality and misinformation.

Contested reporting can contain propaganda, misinformation, and selective framing, so systems must combine access to diverse narratives with source assessment and verification of contested claims. Future evaluations should examine how models preserve competing perspectives while distinguishing reliable evidence from unsupported or misleading accounts. NarrativeBench may contains narratives which could be considered as misinformation in some regions; The authors of the paper do not endorse the narratives as factual accounts of events.

Citation coverage and claim support.

We measure narrative representation through citations to supplied articles, and our citation-support audit examines whether cited sources support the associated claims in a sample of responses (Appendix C.1). Extending assessment across responses and languages, including how faithfully responses convey the causes and interpretations each account emphasizes, would connect narrative coverage to the reliability of the information users receive. However, this is not trivial, LLM accounts can cause information loss, where the meaning, strength of argument and emotion might change. Measuring these information losses is a complex topic that requires interpreting the downstream effect of a give narrative.

Human evaluation of higher-level capabilities.

Evaluating the effects of the higher-level capabilities on filter bubbles, echo chambers, and linguistic disparities requires human-subject studies of information seeking. For instance, even when models present competing accounts, users may selectively attend to perspectives that support existing beliefs [41]. Future studies should examine whether improvements in narrative coverage, robustness to confirmatory queries, and information parity broaden the perspectives of users from different regions and languages consider and mitigate the phenomenons of echo chambers, filter bubbles and cultural barriers to develop common ground.

Information seeking across multiple turns.

NarrativeBench evaluates responses to fixed queries and instructions, including a follow-up request to recover narratives omitted from a supplied answer. During a conversation, users revise their goals, introduce evidence, and change which perspectives they want to explore. Multi-turn evaluation should test how models develop the narratives and support narrative consumption across evolving intents and instructions.

Information consumption.

Effective information seeking requires people to understand and use the information models provide. Benchmark evaluations should incorporate user studies to examine how the organization, detail, and pacing of narrative presentation affect users’ ability to compare accounts and investigate their sources. Accounting for differences in prior knowledge, language proficiency, and available attention would help develop systems that make diverse information both accessible and usable.

Appendix A Dataset Construction and Validation

A.1 Article Collection and Coverage

We gathered news articles through localized searches combining topic names, involved actors and region-specific terms in the relevant publication languages. Searches used Google Advanced Search, Yandex and Baidu, with source-domain and date filters where appropriate; country-specific routing supported localized retrieval where available. We screened articles for topical relevance, accessible body text and identifiable sources, then organized the articles by topic, source perspective and publication language. The corpus contains 1,333 articles representing 180 narrative groups across 23 topics, with coverage summarized in Table 3.

A.2 Narrative Diversity

We compared multilingual embeddings of all 1,333 article texts across the 23 topics, measuring the difference between mean cosine similarity for articles from the same narrative group and articles from different groups within each topic. Articles within the same group were more similar, with an equally weighted mean difference across topics of 0.047 (95% bootstrap CI [0.044,0.051][0.044,0.051], permutation p<.001p<.001). After restricting comparisons to the same publication language, articles from the same source perspective remained more similar than articles from different perspectives (mean difference 0.012, 95% CI [0.009,0.015][0.009,0.015]).

We encoded original-language texts with multilingual-e5-base, dividing each article into chunks within the encoder’s input limit and averaging normalized chunk embeddings with content-token weights. Confidence intervals use 5,000 topic-level bootstrap samples; permutation tests use 1,999 label shuffles within topics, preserving publication-language strata for the same-language comparison. English-text checks on 1,283 articles also found higher similarity within narrative groups: the mean difference was 0.067 with all-mpnet-base-v2 (95% CI [0.053,0.083][0.053,0.083]) and 0.012 with multilingual-e5-base (95% CI [0.010,0.015][0.010,0.015]); both permutation p<.001p<.001.

A.3 Query Construction and Plausibility

Reddit queries were gathered through topic-specific searches, providing 283 directly sourced questions; adapting Reddit question structures to topics with limited coverage supplied 177 queries. The 460-query set contains 230 neutral and 230 confirmatory queries to evaluate narrative coverage under both open information requests and requests that favor a particular interpretation or outcome.

Two independent annotators outside the research team rated a sample of 100 English queries, comprising 86 adaptations and 14 directly sourced questions, on how likely a person would be to ask each query to an AI assistant. Mean ratings were 4.09 and 4.89 on a five-point scale, and neither annotator rated a query as unlikely or very unlikely. Both rated 66 of the 100 queries as likely or very likely; ratings differed in severity, with 39% exact agreement and weighted Cohen’s κ=−0.067\kappa=-0.067.

A.4 Query Languages and Translation Quality

The query set provides 11,038 query–language versions across 24 languages: Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Bengali, Chinese, Dari, English, French, German, Hebrew, Hindi, Nepali, Persian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Tamil, Thai, Tigrinya, Turkish, Ukrainian and Urdu. Article publication languages comprise the same set apart from Thai. We prepared translations with Google Translate in Google Sheets and the Google Translate website for Dari and Tigrinya.

We assessed 1,704 translations of 213 English queries into eight target languages using WMT22-COMETKiwi-DA [49]; mean scores ranged from 0.853 to 0.879 across languages. Independent annotators contributed 132 ratings of 40 query–translation pairs selected across languages and translation-quality bands. Annotators compared each translation with the English query and rated meaning preservation and the likelihood of a person asking the translated query to an AI assistant; participants received $12 for the approximately five-minute task.

Annotators found that translations preserved meaning in 90.8% of the ratings they could assess (118/130) and that the queries were likely to be asked by a person in 89.0% (113/127). Positive ratings combine fully or mostly preserved meaning and likely or very likely query plausibility. Tables 4 and 5 report the language and quality-band results.

Translation quality and performance

Across 17,901 responses covering 754 query–language pairs from 189 queries in eight languages, translation quality had no detectable association with benchmark performance (Pearson r=−0.019r=-0.019, p=.596p=.596; Spearman ρ=−0.007\rho=-0.007, p=.848p=.848). A regression controlling for question, model-by-language, task and context composition estimated a 0.17-percentage-point increase in the task score per 0.01 COMETKiwi increase (95% CI [−0.15,0.49][-0.15,0.49], p=.297p=.297). Benchmark scores showed no clear gradient across the observed translation-quality range.

A.5 Data and Code Availability

We release the articles, queries, evaluation cases and 72,000 model responses with the instructions, prior answers, response-language labels and code needed to reproduce the scores. Document IDs link citations to articles and narratives, while query IDs link translated versions of the same question. The accompanying README explains how to load the data, prepare model inputs and reproduce the scores, while the dataset card records the release license and publisher attribution for article texts.

Appendix B Evaluation Details

B.1 Evaluation Cases

The evaluation covers all 460 queries through 960 query–language pairs, each assessed under NI, NE, MNI, BP and DP, producing 4,800 cases per configuration. Each task contains 480 neutral and 480 confirmatory cases, and each query language contributes 40 questions across all 23 topics. Of the 460 queries, 420 appear in two languages and 40 in three.

The document context contains three articles from each selected narrative, producing contexts of 9–45 articles with a median of 24. Article selection remains fixed for each query across tasks and query languages, and instructions are provided in the query language. For MNI, a fixed prior answer presents one designated narrative using its three articles; the same prior answer is supplied to every evaluated model. The release includes the prior answers and their generation settings.

B.2 Model Settings and Generation Costs

We evaluate 14 models under 15 configurations, including two reasoning and output-budget settings for GPT-OSS 20B. Table 6 reports model identities and settings; comparisons examine model size, base versus instruction-tuned variants, and reasoning settings within model families.

Local inference ran on H200 GPUs using vLLM with four concurrent sequences and a maximum of 8,192 batched tokens; Slurm jobs requested 24 CPUs and 200 GB of host memory. For a complete 4,800-case evaluation on one H200, Qwen3.5 0.8B IT, Gemma 4 26B IT and Qwen3.5 9B IT used approximately 2.29, 4.19 and 5.60 GPU-hours, respectively.

OpenAI requests were submitted through batch_controller.py using the Batch API. At November 2026 API rates, recorded token usage gives estimated costs of $80.15 for GPT-5.4 mini and $14.48 for GPT-6 Luna, each covering 4,800 cases with applicable batch and caching discounts. Recorded shared prior-answer generation adds approximately $5.06, bringing the combined estimate to about $100 for the two evaluations and prior generation.

B.3 Language Validation and Scoring

We identify response language using Lingua, with fastText language identification for Amharic, Tigrinya, Nepali and Dari, and review ambiguous flags before scoring. Responses identified as using a different language or mixing languages receive zero; other responses proceed to citation-based evaluation. NI and NE use narrative F1, while MNI, BP and DP use narrative recall, as defined in the main evaluation section. The released scorer includes the detection rules and scoring implementation.

B.4 HC-2: Signed Adjusted Comparison

To examine whether narrative coverage is higher or lower under confirmatory queries, we regress BP/DP narrative recall on query category for each configuration, accounting for topic, query language and prompt condition. Table 7 reports confirmatory-minus-neutral differences with question-clustered standard errors; positive estimates indicate higher recall under confirmatory queries, and negative estimates indicate lower recall.

B.5 Source-Language Omission

We count a source language as omitted when the document context includes articles in that language and the answer cites none of them. Comparing the same questions, contexts, models and prompts covers 215 question–source-language pairs from 181 questions. Source-language omission averages 41.3% when query and source languages match and 50.4% otherwise, with lower matching-language omission for 22 of the 23 source languages. Figure 2 reports omission rates and question counts for each source language.

Appendix C Independent Validation and Robustness Checks

C.1 Citation Support

Two independent annotators assessed whether source articles supported 45 cited sentences, with five pairs sampled per query language across nine languages. The sample combined 20 pairs selected across preliminary support categories with 25 pairs added to fill coverage gaps. Annotators read English versions of each sentence and source article and rated support as full, partial, absent or contradictory. The audit selected the first citation to a required narrative from each sampled response across the nine query languages.

Annotators agreed on 37 of 45 pairs (82.2%; Cohen’s κ=0.708\kappa=0.708, weighted κ=0.866\kappa=0.866). They found at least partial support in 34 and 36 pairs, respectively, including 33 pairs supported according to both annotators. Table 8 reports the query-language breakdown.

C.2 Citation Selection and Context Length

We examined citation selection in a supplementary evaluation of 1,720 cases across 12 models, comparing observed citations with selecting no documents, all documents, or a random set matched to the observed citation count. Models scored above random selection on NI and below random selection on NE, MNI, BP and DP (Table 9).

Across these cases, input length ranged from 11,048 to 122,167 tokens. A regression controlling for model, task, query language and question estimated a 4.3-percentage-point change in the task score per doubling of input length (95% CI [−0.7,9.3][-0.7,9.3]), with no detectable decline after accounting for the task and question composition. A complete-panel check across six models estimated a similar change of 3.4 percentage points (95% CI [−3.1,9.8][-3.1,9.8]).

C.3 Generation Settings and Narrative Coverage

We compared GPT-5.4-mini with medium and no reasoning on 985 identical inputs, holding the 3,000-token output cap fixed while sampling settings differed. With medium reasoning, NI F1 increased from 28.11% to 39.37%, while NE F1 and MNI, BP and DP recall decreased by 7.38–15.94 percentage points. Of the medium-reasoning responses, 102 exhausted the output cap, including 46 empty answers; all responses remained in the evaluation.

Separate comparisons of 985 identical-input pairs per Gemini model varied thinking settings and output caps together. Under the minimum settings, Flash scores decreased by 8.09–10.59 percentage points across the five tasks, while Pro scores decreased by 0.43–6.38 points. The GPT-OSS 20B comparison in Table 1 also varies reasoning effort and output budget together. Generation settings change narrative selection and coverage differently across tasks, making their reporting alongside model identity important for interpreting performance.

C.4 Performance on Post-Cutoff Evidence

We examined whether models covered narratives less effectively when the supplied articles were published after their documented knowledge cutoffs. Publication dates were available for 366 articles in a 588-article analysis sample. Across nine models and 11,996 responses, recall showed no detectable decline as the share of post-cutoff articles increased (estimated change from entirely pre-cutoff to entirely post-cutoff dated evidence: +4.77+4.77 percentage points, SE 4.844.84, p=.325p=.325). The regression compares the same document contexts across models while accounting for differences between models and contexts.

C.5 Queries from Conversation Logs

Keyword and embedding-based searches of first user messages in WildChat and ShareChat yielded 14 queries retained for evaluation, comprising 11 from WildChat and three from ShareChat. We evaluated the queries under BP using the benchmark’s document contexts. Narrative recall was 46.4% (SE 7.5%) for GPT-5.4 and 46.8% (SE 9.0%) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, showing the same pattern of incomplete narrative coverage observed in the benchmark.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: In this paper we ground the benchmark to evaluate the ability of models to support information seeking across diverse multilingual narratives. To enable this we provide three artifacts: first, we source and provide a dataset of 1,333 articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics. This provides us ecological validity and furthermore even our questions are grounded by questions asked in Reddit.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We provide a explicit limitations sections where we highlight the limitations of the paper and the practical considerations that should be taken into account to analyze the results of the paper.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: Paper does not make a theory contribution.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: The paper describes dataset construction, task definitions, model configurations and scoring, with the evaluation cases, responses and replay code prepared for release.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: We provide the code and data needed to reproduce the benchmark. Furthermore, we provide a README detailing the steps needed to run the benchmark and we also provide a validation script to validate the local setup.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: The dataset and benchmark section of the paper details the models chosen, the hyperparameter, the process of gathering the dataset, and rationales behind the design decisions.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: We provide Standard Errors for each reported result. We also highlight the NarrativeBench@4K sample that we test on and it’s representativeness.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: Appendix B.2 reports model configurations and output budgets.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: We follow the NeurIPS Code of Ethics to the best of our knowledge. We ensure that all our data was publicly available and no personally identifiable information was contained in the dataset by design. We highlight the limitations, the potential harms and usecases for the dataset and benchmark explicitly. We also ensure that our dataset and code is accessible and easy to use for all researchers.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: We detail the implications of our work in the discussion section and also highlight the potential negative impacts in the limitations section.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [Yes]

  54. Justification: The Limitations section discusses narrative representation and source quality; the dataset card records source attribution and article rights.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: Appendix A.5 describes source attribution and the release license. To comply with the copyright of different websites, we ensure that our work comes under fair use and apply the “cc-by-nc-sa-4.0” license to our repository that restricts commercial use and only allows use and reproduction for non-commercial research use cases which come under fair use. Furthermore, in the documents.parquet file we attribute the content by providing the url to the source in the “url” column. We have also included responsible use in the repository.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: We detail the dataset construction, the design choices, the benchmark and the rationale behind it. We provide excerpts in the Appendix and a detailed README for the assets.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [Yes]

  69. Justification: Appendices A.3, A.4 and C.1 report annotation instructions and outcomes. Translation-quality participants were paid $12 for an approximately five-minute task.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [Yes]

  74. Justification: The annotation study received an IRB exemption.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  79. Justification: Generation settings for query adaptations and MNI prior answers accompany the evaluation code and fixed inputs.

  80. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.

    • •

      Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
